title: Writing by rolling dice
objectives: Generate text by picking each next word from its probabilities with a random number.

screens.title: Fair picks
screens.prose: To write, we pick each next word at random, but fairly: each word as often as its chance. Three people pick a word after “the” from this row. They get cat, dog and cat.

state.caption: The row for “the” as chances ($\tfrac16$ is drawn as 0.17).

screens.question: Did all three pick fairly?

options.text: They may all be fair: any word in the row can come
Only the two who got cat: fair means the top word
options.why: That is always taking the top word, not picking at random. A fair pick gives dog its chance of $\tfrac16$.

options.text: None of them: fair picks from one row must agree
options.why: Random picks differ from one to the next. Only over many picks does cat come about half the time.

hints.text: Can a fair pick ever give dog?
dog has a chance of $\tfrac16$, not 0.
Yes, one time in six, so a dog in three picks is no surprise.

feedback.generic: Not quite. A fair pick can give any word with a chance above 0.

byKey.top: Taking cat every time is not random. A fair picker gives dog one time in six.
byKey.agree: Fair random picks differ. Only the share over many picks follows the chances.

explain.text: A fair pick gives cat half the time and dog one time in six, so one dog in three picks is no surprise. Different picks are the point: that is how a table writes different sentences.

screens.title: A number from 0 to 1
screens.prose: The line from 0 to 1 is cut into one piece per word, each as long as that word's chance. Drag $u$ and read the word it lands in.

derive.caption: $u$ is {{fixed(u.x, 2)}}: it lands in {{u.x < 0.5 ? 'cat' : u.x < 2/3 ? 'mat' : u.x < 5/6 ? 'jam' : 'dog'}}.

screens.question: Drag $u$ to 0.62. Which word does it land in?

options.why: 0.62 is past $\tfrac12$, the end of cat's piece.
jam's piece starts at $\tfrac23$, about 0.667, and 0.62 is before it.
dog's piece starts at $\tfrac56$, about 0.833.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the piece that holds 0.62.

explain.text: 0.62 is past $\tfrac12$ but before $\tfrac23$, so it lands in mat. Cat's piece is half the line, so a random $u$ lands there half the time.

screens.title: Sampling
screens.prose: You just **sampled**: draw a random number $u$ from 0 to 1, then walk along the **running totals** $\tfrac12, \tfrac23, \tfrac56, 1$. The word is the first whose running total is above $u$.
screens.question: Tap the word that $u = 0.9$ picks.

hints.text: Walk the running totals until one is above 0.9.
jam's running total is $\tfrac56$, about 0.833.
0.833 is below 0.9, so walk on: the total 1 is above it, so dog.

feedback.correct: dog: the first running total above 0.9 is 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the first running total above 0.9.

byKey.jam: jam's running total, $\tfrac56 \approx 0.833$, is below 0.9, so walk on to dog.
byKey.cat: cat's piece ends at $\tfrac12$; 0.9 is far past it.

explain.text: The running totals are 0.5, about 0.667, about 0.833 and 1. The first above 0.9 is 1, so $u = 0.9$ picks dog.

screens.title: A running total
screens.prose: Each running total adds the next chance: $\tfrac12$, then $\tfrac12 + \tfrac16 = \tfrac23$, then one more $\tfrac16$, and so on.
screens.question: What is the running total after jam? Give a fraction.

hints.text: Add cat's, mat's and jam's chances.
jam's piece ends here.
$\tfrac12 + \tfrac16 + \tfrac16 = \tfrac56$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add every chance up to and including jam.

byKey.own: That is jam's own chance. A running total adds every chance up to and including jam.
byKey.all: 1 is the total after dog, the last word.

explain.text: $\tfrac12 + \tfrac16 + \tfrac16 = \tfrac56$. So jam's piece runs from $\tfrac23$ to $\tfrac56$, and $u$ picks jam when it falls in between.

screens.title: Writing by hand
screens.prose: Start at “the” and use three random numbers in turn: 0.1, 0.5, 0.9. The rows you need are below; cat's running totals are $\tfrac13, \tfrac23, 1$.
screens.question: Which four words does it write?

options.why: After “cat”, 0.5 is above sat's running total, $\tfrac13$, so walk on to ate.
You used the numbers in reverse order. 0.1 comes first, and it picks cat.
0.5 is below ate's running total, $\tfrac23$, so it stops at ate.

hints.text: Use 0.1 on the row for “the”.
Then use 0.5 on the row for “cat”.
0.1 picks cat; 0.5 picks ate; after ate only “the” can come.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Use one number per word, in order.

byKey.sat: 0.5 is above $\tfrac13$, so sat is passed and ate is picked.
byKey.dog: The first number is 0.1, which picks cat.

explain.text: 0.1 picks cat, since $\tfrac12$ is above 0.1. Then 0.5 is above $\tfrac13$ but below $\tfrac23$, so ate. After “ate” the only word is “the”, whatever 0.9 is.

screens.title: Four runs
screens.prose: A script repeats this, drawing each $u$ with Python's `random.Random(7)`. The seed, 7, fixes the numbers, so the runs come out the same every time. Here are four runs of 12 words.

params.title: Seed 7: four runs from “the”
lines: the cat sat on the mat . the mat . the cat
the cat ate the cat sat on the mat . the cat
the dog sat on the cat . the mat . the mat
the cat sat on the cat sat on the cat . the

screens.question: Is any pair of neighbouring words in these runs missing from the text?

options.text: No: every pair is a pair from the text
Yes: “ate the cat” never appears in the text
options.why: That is three words. The table only promises each pair, “ate the” and “the cat”, and both are in the text.

options.text: Yes: these runs are not sentences in the text
options.why: The runs are new, but each step is a pair the text holds. New sentences from old pairs is what the table does.

hints.text: Where does each next word come from?
Check the second run pair by pair.
Each word comes from the row of the word before, so every pair was counted in the text.

feedback.correct: No: every neighbouring pair is in the text.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check pairs, not longer runs.

byKey.triple: “ate the cat” is new as three words, but both of its pairs are in the text.

explain.text: Each step picks a word from the row of the word before, so every neighbouring pair comes from the text. The runs as a whole are new: “the cat ate the cat sat on the mat” is not in the text.

screens.title: Always the top word
screens.prose: A friend says the best writer skips the random number and always takes the most likely word. On a tie it takes the word met first in the text, so “sat” after “cat”.
screens.question: Which 8 words does that writer write, starting at “the”?

options.text: the cat sat on the cat sat on
the cat sat on the mat . the
options.why: That copies the text. After “on” comes “the”, and the top word after “the” is always cat, never mat.

options.text: the cat ate the jam . the dog
options.why: Those are random picks. The top word after “cat” is the first of the tie, sat, every time.

hints.text: What is the top word after “the”? After “cat”?
cat has the biggest chance after “the”.
the, cat, sat, on, and “on” leads back to “the”.

feedback.correct: It loops: the cat sat on the cat sat on.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Take the top word every time.

byKey.copy: After “on” comes “the”, then cat again: it never reaches mat.
byKey.random: No random number is used, so ate, jam and dog never come.

explain.text: Always taking the top word loops: “the cat sat on”, then back to “the”. Random picks are what let the table leave the loop and reach mat, jam or dog.

screens.title: Off the end
screens.prose: The rule takes the first running total *above* $u$. But a computer stores $\tfrac16$ rounded to about 16 digits, so the running total of the four chances ends a hair short of 1.
screens.question: A random $u$ can be `0.9999999999999999`, and no running total is above it. What should the picker do?

options.why: Then the writer stops mid-sentence. This $u$ is in dog's piece; only the rounding left it out.
That gives cat a little extra chance. This $u$ belongs to the last piece.

hints.text: Which piece of the line does a $u$ just under 1 belong to?
The last line shows the total falls short of 1.
It belongs to dog, the last word, so return dog.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Think about which piece this $u$ is in.

byKey.none: Returning nothing would end the run early. Fall back to the last word.

explain.text: The true total is 1, but each $\tfrac16$ is stored rounded, so the sum falls short by a hair. A picker that runs off the end must return the last word. Rounding like this comes back in `py-found`.

screens.title: Picking in code
screens.prose: `words` and `chances` are lists in the same order, such as the row for “the”.
screens.question: Write `pick(words, chances, u)`: return the first word whose running total is above `u`, or the last word if none is.

widget.starter:
def pick(words, chances, u):
    return words[0]
widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected word exactly.

mutants.symptom: Uses at-or-above instead of above, so u = 0.5 picks cat instead of mat.
Returns nothing when rounding leaves the running total just under u, instead of the last word.
Compares u with each chance on its own instead of the running total.

hints.text: Keep a running total and add one chance at a time.
Return `words[i]` as soon as `u < total`; after the loop, return `words[-1]`.

feedback.correct: Your picker walks the running totals and falls back to the last word.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: 0.5 is not above $\tfrac12$: use `u < total`, so 0.5 goes on to mat.
byKey.test-6: No running total is above this `u`. Return `words[-1]` after the loop.

explain.text:
Add each chance to a running total and stop at the first total above `u`. If rounding leaves the last total just short, the loop ends and the last word is returned.

```python
total = 0
for i in range(len(words)):
    total = total + chances[i]
    if u < total:
        return words[i]
return words[-1]
```

screens.title: Writing in code
screens.prose: `TABLE` is the course table. `row_for(TABLE, word)` gives a word's row as two lists, `words` and `chances`. Your `pick` is in the starter.
screens.question: Write `generate(table, start, us)`: start at `start`, pick one word for each `u` in `us`, and return every word in a list.

tests.setup:
import random
rng = random.Random(7)
skip = [rng.random() for _ in range(11)]
us = [rng.random() for _ in range(11)]
tests.expect: 'the cat ate the cat sat on the mat . the cat'

widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected list of words exactly.

mutants.symptom: Looks up the row of the start word every time instead of the word just written.
Always takes the most likely word instead of sampling with u.
Leaves the start word out of the list it returns.

hints.text: Keep the word now in a variable that starts at `start`.
For each `u`: get the row of the word now, pick, append, and make the pick the word now.

feedback.correct: Your writer walks the table one word at a time.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: 0.1, 0.5, 0.9 from “the” should write the cat ate the. Look up the row of the word just written each time.
byKey.test-3: With no numbers the list is just the start word.

explain.text:
Keep the word now; for each $u$, look up its row, pick, and append. The last test is the second run of the seed-7 console, so your writer and the script agree.

```python
for u in us:
    words, chances = row_for(table, word)
    word = pick(words, chances, u)
    out.append(word)
```

screens.title: Sampling in one rule
screens.prose: To sample from a row: $$\text{word} = \text{first word whose running total is above } u$$ with $u$ a random number from 0 to 1, and the last word if rounding leaves none. Over many picks, each word comes up about as often as its chance says.
screens.question: Out of 600 picks after “the”, about how many give cat?

hints.text: What share of the line is cat's piece?
Half of 600 is 300.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply cat's chance by 600.

byKey.even: 150 shares the picks evenly between four words. Cat's chance is $\tfrac12$.
byKey.dog: 100 is $\tfrac16$ of 600, the count for each of the other words.

explain.text: Cat's piece is half the line, so about half the picks, 300 of 600, land there. Each other word gets about 100.

screens.title: A chatbot's next word
screens.prose: A chatbot writes a reply one piece at a time in just this way, with the table replaced by a big network. Drafting a market note, after “The FTSE” its chances are rose 0.55, fell 0.35 and closed 0.10.
screens.question: With $u = 0.6$, which word does it write?

options.why: 0.6 is above rose's running total, 0.55, so walk on.
closed's piece starts at 0.9. fell's running total, 0.9, is already above 0.6.

hints.text: Work out the running totals.
rose ends at 0.55.
0.55, 0.9, 1: the first above 0.6 is 0.9, fell.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the first running total above 0.6.

explain.text: The running totals are 0.55, 0.9 and 1. The first above 0.6 is 0.9, so it writes fell, whatever the market did. `ai-use` level 1 shows how such a network is trained.

ideas: To sample, draw a random $u$ from 0 to 1 and take the first word whose running total is above $u$.
Each word then comes up about as often as its chance, so different runs write different sentences from the same pairs.
Always taking the top word loops; and a picker returns the last word when rounding leaves the total just under 1.
